items.zh: 云何鼻識自性？謂依鼻，了別香。彼所依者，俱有依，謂鼻。等無間依，謂意。種子依，謂一切種子阿賴耶識。鼻，謂四大種所造鼻識所依淨色，無見有對。
items.en: What is the self-nature of the nose-consciousness? It is the discerning of smell in dependence on the nose. Its support: the co-existent support is the nose; the immediately-preceding support is the manas; the seed support is the all-seeds ālayavijñāna. The nose is the pure form, made of the four great elements, on which the nose-consciousness depends — invisible, yet with obstruction.
The manas and the seeds are as explained before.

items.zh: 彼所緣者，謂香、無見有對。此復多種。謂好香、惡香、平等香，鼻所嗅知根、莖、華、葉、果、實之香。如是等類，有眾多香。
items.en: Its object is smell — invisible, yet with obstruction. This again has many kinds: pleasant smell, unpleasant smell, and neutral smell; and the smells the nose discerns in roots, stems, flowers, leaves, and fruit. Smells of this and other such kinds are many.

items.zh: 又香者，謂鼻所聞、鼻所取、鼻所嗅等差別之名。是鼻所行、鼻境界，鼻識所行、鼻識境界、鼻識所緣，意識所行、意識境界、意識所緣。助伴及業，如前應知。
items.en: Smell, again, has these further names: what the nose smells, what the nose takes in, what the nose senses, among other such distinctions. It is what the nose operates on, the nose's realm; what the nose-consciousness operates on, its realm, and its object; and what the mental consciousness operates on, its realm, and its object. Its accompaniments and activity should be understood as before.

items.zh: 云何舌識自性？謂依舌，了別味。彼所依者，俱有依，謂舌。等無間依，謂意。種子依，謂一切種子阿賴耶識。舌，謂四大種所造舌識所依淨色，無見有對。
items.en: What is the self-nature of the tongue-consciousness? It is the discerning of taste in dependence on the tongue. Its support: the co-existent support is the tongue; the immediately-preceding support is the manas; the seed support is the all-seeds ālayavijñāna. The tongue is the pure form, made of the four great elements, on which the tongue-consciousness depends — invisible, yet with obstruction.
The manas and the seeds are as explained before.

items.zh: 彼所緣者，謂味，無見有對。此復多種。謂苦、酢、辛、甘、鹹、淡、可意、不可意、若捨處所，舌所甞。
items.en: Its object is taste — invisible, yet with obstruction. This again has many kinds: bitter, sour, pungent, sweet, salty, and bland; and agreeable, disagreeable, and neutral — these are what the tongue tastes.

items.zh: 又味者，謂應甞、應吞、應噉、應飲、應舐、應吮、應受用，如是等差別之名。是舌所行、舌境界，舌識所行、舌識境界、舌識所緣，意識所行、意識境界、意識所緣。助伴及業，如前應知。
items.en: Taste, again, has these further names: what is to be tasted, swallowed, chewed, drunk, licked, sucked, or consumed, among other such distinctions. It is what the tongue operates on, the tongue's realm; what the tongue-consciousness operates on, its realm, and its object; and what the mental consciousness operates on, its realm, and its object. Its accompaniments and activity should be understood as before.

items.zh: 云何身識自性？謂依身，了別觸。彼所依者，俱有依，謂身。等無間依，謂意。種子依，謂一切種子阿賴耶識。身，謂四大種所造身識所依淨色，無見有對。
items.en: What is the self-nature of the body-consciousness? It is the discerning of the tangible in dependence on the body. Its support: the co-existent support is the body; the immediately-preceding support is the manas; the seed support is the all-seeds ālayavijñāna. The body is the pure form, made of the four great elements, on which the body-consciousness depends — invisible, yet with obstruction.
The manas and the seeds are as explained before.

items.zh: 彼所緣者，謂觸，無見有對。此復多種。謂地、水、火、風、輕性、重性、滑性、澁性、冷、飢、渴、飽、力、劣、緩、急、病、老、死、蛘、悶、粘、疲、息、軟怯、勇，如是等類，有眾多觸。
items.en: Its object is the tangible — invisible, yet with obstruction. This again has many kinds: earth, water, fire, and wind; lightness and heaviness; smoothness and roughness; cold; hunger, thirst, and fullness; strength and weakness; slowness and urgency; sickness, old age, and death; itching, faintness, stickiness, fatigue, and rest; softness; timidity and courage. Tangibles of this and other such kinds are many.

items.zh: 此復三種。謂好觸、惡觸、捨處所觸、身所觸。又觸者，謂所摩、所觸、若鞕、若軟、若動、若煖，如是等差別之名。
items.en: This, again, is threefold: agreeable touch, disagreeable touch, and touch that is neither — these are what the body touches. The tangible, again, has these further names: what is rubbed, what is touched, hardness, softness, movement, and warmth, among other such distinctions.

items.zh: 是身所行，身境界，身識所行、身識境界、身識所緣，意識所行、意識境界、意識所緣。助伴及業、如前應知。
items.en: It is what the body operates on, the body's realm; what the body-consciousness operates on, its realm, and its object; and what the mental consciousness operates on, its realm, and its object. Its accompaniments and activity should be understood as before.

items.title: How the Five Consciousnesses Actually Arise

items.zh: 復次，雖眼不壞，色現在前，能生作意若不正起，所生眼識必不得生。要眼不壞，色現在前，能生作意正復現起，所生眼識方乃得生。如眼識生，乃至身識，應知亦爾。
items.en: Further: even where the eye is unimpaired and form stands present before it, if the attention that would give rise to the eye-consciousness does not properly arise, then the eye-consciousness that would be produced does not arise at all. Only where the eye is unimpaired, form stands present before it, and the attention that would give rise to the eye-consciousness does properly arise, does the eye-consciousness that would be produced actually arise. As with the arising of the eye-consciousness, so it should be understood with the ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses.

items.zh: 復次，由眼識生，三心可得。如其次第，謂率爾心、尋求心、決定心。初是眼識，二在意識。
items.en: Further: with the arising of the eye-consciousness, three minds may be found, in this order — the sudden mind, the seeking mind, and the deciding mind. The first belongs to the eye-consciousness; the latter two belong to the mental consciousness.

items.zh: 決定心後方有染淨。此後乃有等流眼識善不善轉。而彼不由自分別力，乃至此意不趣餘境，經爾所時，眼意二識或善或染，相續而轉。如眼識生，乃至身識，應知亦爾。
items.en: Only after the deciding mind is there the defiled or pure mind. After this, then, the eye-consciousness turns, in like flow, towards the wholesome or the unwholesome — yet not through any discriminating power of its own. For as long as this mental consciousness does not turn towards some other object, the eye-consciousness and the mental consciousness, wholesome or defiled, continue turning in unbroken succession. As with the arising of the eye-consciousness, so it should be understood with the ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses.

items.title: Two Similes, and the Stage's Close

items.zh: 復次，應觀五識所依，如往餘方者所乘。所緣，如所為事。助伴，如同侶。業，如自功能。
items.en: Further: the five consciousnesses' support should be seen as like the vehicle of one travelling to another place; their object, like the business for which he travels; their accompaniments, like his companions; and their activity, like his own working capacity.

items.zh: 復有差別。應觀五識所依，如居家者家。所緣，如所受用。助伴，如僕使等。業，如作用。
items.en: There is, further, another distinction. The five consciousnesses' support should be seen as like a householder's house; their object, like what he makes use of within it; their accompaniments, like his servants and attendants; and their activity, like his own actions.

items.zh: 已說五識身相應地。云何意地？
items.en: The Stage Corresponding to the Body of the Five Sense Consciousnesses has now been explained. What is the Mind Stage?

blocks.text: Today finishes the first of the seventeen stages. The nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses follow the eye-consciousness's pattern closely, so the first half of the reading moves quickly. Then come two of the most practically important passages in fascicle 1: what must be present for a sense consciousness to arise at all, and the sequence of "five minds" that unfolds in a single act of seeing. The stage ends with two similes. One short phrase, 意及種子，如前分別 ("the manas and the seeds are as explained before"), is missing from Ru-Yi in each of the nose, tongue, and body sections; we have supplied it. It simply refers back to Day 1.

The lists are concrete on purpose. The nose knows pleasant, unpleasant, and neutral smells, and the smells of roots, stems, flowers, leaves, and fruit; the tongue knows bitter, sour, pungent, sweet, salty, and bland. The "further names" for taste, to be tasted, swallowed, chewed, drunk, licked, sucked, consumed, sort taste by the way it is taken in. The point is not botany or cookery. It is to show that each consciousness has its own field and no other: the nose-consciousness never tastes, and the tongue-consciousness never smells.

subs.head: The tangible, and why "old age" is something you touch

blocks.text: The body-consciousness's object, the **tangible** (觸, *spraṣṭavya*), includes the four great elements (earth, water, fire, and wind, here felt as hardness, wetness, warmth, and movement) and a long list of derived tangibles: lightness and heaviness, smoothness and roughness, cold, hunger, thirst, fullness, strength and weakness, sickness, old age, death, itching, fatigue, rest.

Some of these are surprising. How can old age or death be touched? Master Cháng Bǎi flags this as a terminology trap: "old age" and "death" here are bodily sensations, physical conditions of the four elements, and not the same terms as the "ageing and death" of the twelve links of dependent origination met later in the treatise. The *Pīxún jì* adds that, apart from the four great elements themselves, which are real, everything on the list from lightness and heaviness to timidity and courage is provisionally designated on states of the elements. Venerable Miào Jìng says simply: "'Old age' too is known by touch, and 'death' as well."

subs.head: Three conditions for a sense consciousness

blocks.text: "Even where the eye is unimpaired and form stands present before it, if the attention … does not properly arise, then the eye-consciousness … does not arise at all." Three things must come together: an unimpaired faculty, an object present, and **attention** (作意). Master Cháng Bǎi quotes a Chinese saying: when the mind is not present, one looks and does not see, listens and does not hear (心不在焉，視而不見，聽而不聞).

Venerable Miào Jìng draws out the practical point. Attention "rouses the mental factors that are due to arise" (*Cheng Weishi Lun*). Improper attention calls up greed or anger to meet the object; attention in accordance with truth calls up compassion and wisdom. "We are ordinary beings; the possibility of our becoming noble ones lies right here."
The treatise now describes what happens in a single act of seeing, as a sequence of "minds" (心):

items: **The sudden mind** (率爾心): the first moment of contact, belonging to the eye-consciousness;
**The seeking mind** (尋求心): the mental consciousness asks, as it were, "what is this?";
**The deciding mind** (決定心): the mental consciousness settles what it is;
**The defiled or pure mind** (染淨心): only now does liking, aversion, faith, or kindness arise;
**The flowing-alike mind** (等流心): the defiled or pure state continues in a stream, and the eye-consciousness flows along with it, "yet not through any discriminating power of its own".

blocks.text: Venerable Miào Jìng stresses that the first three are still indeterminate: "When it comes to the defiled-or-pure mind, that is when afflictions arrive." The eye-consciousness does not make itself wholesome or unwholesome; it borrows that quality from the mental consciousness for as long as the mental consciousness stays on the same object.
This is a map of where practice can intervene. Between deciding and reacting, there is a gap, and the quality of what fills it depends on attention.

The five factors are illustrated twice. For a traveller, the support is the vehicle, the object is the business he travels for, the accompaniments are his companions, and the activity is his own working capacity. For a householder, the support is his house, the object what he enjoys there, the accompaniments his servants, and the activity his own actions. Venerable Miào Jìng notes that neither simile gives an image for self-nature; the self-nature is the traveller or householder himself, the one who uses all the rest.

Master Cháng Bǎi draws the conclusion of the whole stage: it is the treatise's first demonstration of non-self. There is no separate "I" that sees, hears, or touches; there are only these five factors arising together, moment by moment, in dependence on conditions. Venerable Miào Jìng adds that once you understand the seed support, you know consciousness arises moment by moment, "so where is any permanent true mind?"

quiz.q: The treatise lists six basic tastes known by the tongue-consciousness. What are they?
options: bitter, sour, pungent, sweet, salty, and bland
bitter, sour, sweet, spicy, astringent, and fragrant
agreeable, disagreeable, neutral, good, bad, and even
tasting, swallowing, chewing, drinking, licking, and sucking
quiz.why: "Its object is taste … bitter, sour, pungent, sweet, salty, and bland; and agreeable, disagreeable, and neutral — these are what the tongue tastes." The six tastes are bitter, sour, pungent, sweet, salty, and bland; agreeable, disagreeable, and neutral, as Master Cháng Bǎi notes, are the sixth consciousness's overlay, not further tastes. D lists the "further names" for taste given in the next sentence, not kinds of taste. "Astringent" and "fragrant" in B are not in the text.

quiz.q: Among the tangibles known by the body-consciousness are "sickness, old age, and death." How should "old age" and "death" be understood here?
options: they are the link of ageing-and-death in the twelve links of dependent origination
they are the mental consciousness's fear of death
they are metaphors, not real tangibles
they are sensations felt through the body — a particular combination or imbalance of the four elements — not the ageing-and-death of the twelve links
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi flags these specifically: "old age" and "death" here are bodily sensations in a technical, physical sense — conditions derived from the four elements — "not the same terms as they appear later in the treatise's account of the twelve links of dependent origination." This is one of the fascicle's terminology traps. The *Pixunji* likewise says that apart from the four great elements themselves, which are real, everything else on the list, from lightness and heaviness to timidity and courage, is provisionally designated on states of the elements. Venerable Miào Jìng says the same: "'Old age' too is known by touch, and 'death' as well." A is the confusion to avoid.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what must be present for the eye-consciousness to arise?
options: it is enough that the eye is unimpaired and form stands present before it
the eye is unimpaired, form stands present before it, and the attention that would give rise to the eye-consciousness does properly arise
attention alone is enough; the eye is not needed
the deciding mind of the mental consciousness must come first
quiz.why: "Even where the eye is unimpaired and form stands present before it, if the attention that would give rise to the eye-consciousness does not properly arise, then the eye-consciousness that would be produced does not arise at all. Only where the eye is unimpaired, form stands present before it, and the attention … does properly arise, does the eye-consciousness … actually arise." A is exactly what the text denies: eyes open, object right there, and still nothing registers if attention does not turn. D reverses the order: the deciding mind comes after the sudden mind.

quiz.q: The treatise says that "with the arising of the eye-consciousness, three minds may be found." To which consciousness does each belong?
options: the sudden mind belongs to the eye-consciousness; the seeking and deciding minds belong to the mental consciousness
all three belong to the eye-consciousness
all three belong to the mental consciousness
the sudden and seeking minds belong to the eye-consciousness; the deciding mind to the mental consciousness
quiz.why: "The sudden mind, the seeking mind, and the deciding mind. The first belongs to the eye-consciousness; the latter two belong to the mental consciousness." The *Pixunji* notes that "may be found" signals that this is not fixed — if the mental consciousness is distracted, all three need not arise. (Note: Master Cháng Bǎi's lecture quotes Venerable Miào Jìng as also calling the sudden mind "the attention factor of the sixth consciousness," which differs from the wording of the text; for examination purposes, follow the text.)

quiz.q: According to Venerable Miào Jìng, at which of the five minds do afflictions first appear?
options: the sudden mind
the seeking mind
the deciding mind
the defiled-or-pure mind — the sudden, seeking, and deciding minds are all still indeterminate; only at the defiled-or-pure mind do afflictions such as craving or anger become active
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "The sudden, seeking, and deciding minds are all still indeterminate. When it comes to the defiled-or-pure mind, that is when afflictions arrive — craving, or anger, all kinds of afflictions become active." The text itself says, "Only after the deciding mind is there the defiled or pure mind." He adds that at the moment of the sudden mind "one cannot yet speak of wholesome or defiled." Master Cháng Bǎi likewise says the eye never judges anything good or bad by itself; it only inherits that judgement from the sixth consciousness.

quiz.q: The treatise compares the five consciousnesses to one travelling to another place. Which pairing is correct?
options: support is like the companions; object is like the vehicle
support is like the business; accompaniments are like the working capacity
activity is like the vehicle; object is like the companions
support is like the vehicle; object like the business for which he travels; accompaniments like his companions; activity like his own working capacity
quiz.why: "The five consciousnesses' support should be seen as like the vehicle of one travelling to another place; their object, like the business for which he travels; their accompaniments, like his companions; and their activity, like his own working capacity." A, B, and C each mismatch the items. Master Cháng Bǎi notes that both similes make the same point: the five factors are not five separate things bolted together, but one working arrangement, the way a traveller's vehicle, errand, companions, and effort all serve a single journey.
